title: Authorization & Access Control
description: Failures in enforcing granular permissions, privilege boundaries, object-level checks, and multi-tenant isolation.

attacks.name: IDOR
attacks.desc: Manipulating direct references to internal database objects (e.g. changing /api/documents/1042 to /api/documents/1043) without server-side validation that the requesting user owns the record.
attacks.prevention: Check object ownership or tenant membership on every request; never treat an object ID as authorization.

attacks.name: BOLA (API object-level)
attacks.desc: API endpoints that expose entity identifiers in URLs and fail to enforce user authorization checks on the target resource, enabling unauthorized data access across tenants.
attacks.prevention: Apply object-level authorization after resolving the requested API resource, including nested and bulk operations.

attacks.name: BFLA (API function-level)
attacks.desc: API controllers that restrict UI buttons but fail to restrict access to administrative endpoints (e.g. PUT /api/v1/users/make_admin) from low-privileged user accounts.
attacks.prevention: Authorize each API function by role and permission on the server, even when the UI hides the action.

attacks.name: Horizontal privilege escalation
attacks.desc: Gaining unauthorized access to private data, profile details, or operational functions belonging to peer accounts operating at the exact same privilege tier.
attacks.prevention: Verify that the authenticated principal owns the requested data; test with two different regular accounts.

attacks.name: Vertical privilege escalation
attacks.desc: Exploiting flawed authorization logic to elevate standard user capabilities to those of a system administrator, compliance officer, or superuser.
attacks.prevention: Enforce privileged operations through server-side roles and explicit policy checks, not client-supplied role values.

attacks.name: Missing function-level access control
attacks.desc: Failing to attach role-based authorization annotations or middleware to server-side business actions, assuming hidden UI navigation provides security.
attacks.prevention: Centralize permission checks for sensitive functions and deny access by default when no policy applies.

attacks.name: Forced browsing
attacks.desc: Accessing restricted resources or administrative modules by manually typing unlinked URLs directly into the browser address bar.
attacks.prevention: Protect every route and resource directly on the server; a hidden link or obscure URL is not a control.

attacks.name: Path traversal / directory traversal
attacks.desc: Supplying dot-dot-slash (../) sequences into file-handling parameters to escape intended web directory boundaries and access arbitrary server operating system files.
attacks.prevention: Resolve and normalize paths before access checks, constrain file operations to an allowlisted directory, and reject escapes.

attacks.name: Parameter tampering
attacks.desc: Altering query strings, hidden HTML form fields, or JSON keys (e.g. 'is_admin': true, 'role': 'manager') to bypass client-side restrictions and influence backend authorization.

attacks.name: HTTP verb tampering
attacks.desc: Switching HTTP methods (e.g. changing a restricted GET request to HEAD, POST, or PUT) to bypass access filters configured exclusively for specific request verbs.

attacks.name: Mass assignment / over-posting
attacks.desc: Submitting unexpected object properties during entity creation or updates that the backend framework automatically binds to internal model fields (e.g. binding 'role': 'admin' or 'verified': true).

attacks.name: Multi-tenant isolation break
attacks.desc: Querying shared multi-tenant databases without mandatory organizational scope filters (e.g. WHERE tenant_id = ?), leaking one corporate customer's proprietary data to another.

attacks.name: Role manipulation via request body
attacks.desc: Injecting role attributes directly inside serialized API payloads during profile updates when the backend fails to sanitize updatable field allowlists.

attacks.name: API version downgrade
attacks.desc: Directing API calls to deprecated API endpoints (e.g. calling /api/v1/auth instead of /api/v2/auth) that remain online but lack recently introduced security controls and rate limits.

attacks.name: Hidden endpoint discovery
attacks.desc: Locating undocumented internal microservice routes and private testing handlers that bypass API gateway authorization policies.

attacks.name: GraphQL introspection leak
attacks.desc: Executing GraphQL introspection queries (__schema, __type) against production endpoints to download the complete schema, queries, mutations, internal types, and field descriptions.

attacks.name: GraphQL field-level auth bypass
attacks.desc: Querying sensitive object fields that lack individual resolver authorization checks even when the parent query or root object was properly authorized.

attacks.name: GraphQL batching attack
attacks.desc: Packaging multiple queries or mutations within a single HTTP request payload to bypass network-level rate limits and execute brute-force attacks against authentication endpoints.

attacks.name: GraphQL alias overloading
attacks.desc: Using GraphQL query aliases to invoke the same intensive mutation or query hundreds of times within a single request, defeating per-request throttling.

attacks.name: GraphQL query depth / complexity DoS
attacks.desc: Submitting deeply nested circular GraphQL queries (e.g. user -> friends -> user -> friends) without server-side depth limits, exhausting server CPU and memory.

attacks.name: GraphQL IDOR
attacks.desc: Manipulating global relay Node IDs or query arguments in GraphQL queries to retrieve unauthorized objects across user boundaries.

attacks.name: Excessive data exposure
attacks.desc: API endpoints returning complete backend database models containing sensitive user fields (hashes, PII, internal IDs) relying entirely on client-side code to filter what gets displayed.

attacks.name: Insecure API key handling
attacks.desc: Transmitting sensitive API keys in query string parameters (where they get logged in server access logs and browser histories) or embedding secret keys in public mobile/web code.

attacks.name: Referer-based access control bypass
attacks.desc: Bypassing authorization controls on backend endpoints that erroneously rely on the client-supplied HTTP Referer header to verify that requests originated from an administrative page.
